  Ice can cover northern rivers for months each winter, and the spring breakup sometimes causes dangerous ice jams. When the jams release, sudden surges of water and ice can damage
  bridges and flood nearby towns.
  
  The Thames winds through the heart of London, where it has been central to the city's trade and identity for nearly two thousand years. Once declared biologically dead, it has
  recovered enough to support seals, eels, and many species of fish.
  
  Rivers transport enormous quantities of dissolved minerals, sand, and clay from the continents to the oceans every year. This sediment builds beaches, deltas, and underwater fans
  along coastlines around the world.
 
  Hydroelectric power plants use the energy of falling or flowing river water to spin turbines and generate electricity. In countries like Norway and Brazil, rivers supply a large
  share of the national power grid.

  The Congo River is the deepest river in the world, with some sections plunging more than two hundred meters below the surface. Its powerful currents and rapids have isolated fish
  populations, leading to remarkable evolutionary diversity.

  River restoration projects aim to undo past damage by removing obsolete dams, replanting banks, and reconnecting floodplains. These efforts often bring back native fish, improve
  water quality, and reduce downstream flooding.

  Many cities were founded at river crossings or confluences, where travel and trade naturally converged. Names like Frankfurt, Oxford, and Pittsburgh still reflect the importance of
  fords and river junctions in their history.

  Underground rivers flow through caves and porous rock, sometimes emerging at springs or disappearing into sinkholes. The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River in the Philippines runs
  for several kilometers beneath a limestone mountain.

  The source of a river is often debated, since many small streams may contribute to its headwaters. Explorers spent centuries searching for the true source of the Nile before
  reaching agreement on its origins.

  Riparian zones are the strips of vegetation along riverbanks that shade the water, stabilize soil, and filter runoff. Healthy riparian forests keep rivers cooler and provide
  crucial habitat for birds, insects, and mammals.

  Rivers have inspired countless poems, songs, and paintings, symbolizing journeys, the passage of time, and constant change. The ancient philosopher Heraclitus famously observed
  that no one ever steps in the same river twice.

  Droughts can shrink mighty rivers to a fraction of their usual size, exposing riverbeds and stranding boats. Low water levels also threaten drinking water supplies, irrigation, and
  the cooling of power plants.

  The Mekong flows through six countries in Southeast Asia and supports one of the largest freshwater fisheries in the world. Its seasonal floods are essential for rice farming and
  for the reproduction of many migratory fish.

  From quiet brooks to massive continental waterways, rivers connect mountains, plains, and oceans in a single flowing system. Protecting them ensures clean water, thriving wildlife,
  and resilient communities for generations to come.
